title: DonasiPlus-Laravel: A Secure, Auditable Dues and Donations Management System for Indonesian Nonprofits

authors.name: Dr. A. Prasetya
authors.affiliation: Department of Computer Engineering, Universitas Indonesia

abstract: Managing membership dues and charitable donations presents recurring operational challenges for Indonesian nonprofit organizations: manual reconciliation, inconsistent receipts, weak audit trails, and payment integration complexity. Existing small-scale solutions either rely on spreadsheets or fragmented third-party services that lack integrated membership management and server-side auditability [1][2][3]. We present DonasiPlus-Laravel, a Laravel 8 based web application engineered for secure, auditable, and scalable management of dues and donations for organizations such as student associations and local NGOs in Jakarta and the Universitas Indonesia ecosystem. Key contributions include (i) an end-to-end payment pipeline integrating Stripe and Midtrans with webhook verification and HMAC checks, (ii) transactional accounting primitives and FIFO reconciliation ensuring consistent ledger balances, (iii) background queue processing with Redis/Horizon for retryable webhooks and exponential backoff to meet 120 ms API targets, and (iv) role-based access control with immutable audit logs. In tests on a 4 vCPU, 8 GB VM and PostgreSQL primary-replica cluster, DonasiPlus achieved 95.4% automated reconciliation accuracy, average API latency $T_{api}=120$ ms, and sustained throughput of 200 transactions per minute under synthetic loads. The system reduces manual reconciliation time by 78% in a six-month pilot at Universitas Indonesia student organizations. Limitations include dependence on third-party gateway SLAs and the need for formal accounting certification for large NGOs; ongoing work targets multi-tenant isolation and formal financial audit integration.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Community organizations, student unions, religious groups, and small non-governmental organizations frequently manage recurring membership dues and irregular donations. In Indonesia, many such groups at universities and local communities in Jakarta rely on manual bookkeeping or disparate payment services that produce inconsistent record-keeping and slow reconciliation. This issue affects transparency, donor trust, and statutory reporting: month-end reconciliation often requires hours of staff time and produces discrepancies between bank statements and internal ledgers. The industry trend toward cloud-hosted payment processors provides opportunities, but safe integration, auditable receipts, and membership-specific workflows remain underdeveloped for Indonesian contexts [1][4].

Prior academic and industrial work has addressed payment integration and nonprofit platforms at different scales. Commercial platforms provide user-facing donation portals but often treat membership dues as an afterthought, lacking fine-grained role control, local gateway support (e.g., Midtrans for Indonesia), and server-side webhook verification [2][5]. Research prototypes emphasize security and throughput for high-volume donations [6][7], but they rarely provide a combined dues-management, recurring billing, and institutional audit trail tailored to university clubs. A practical limitation of prior work is the omission of full-stack implementations that include database replication, background queue semantics, and explicit reconciliation algorithms that map gateway payouts to ledger entries [3][8].

The problem statement is therefore twofold: how to provide an integrated web platform that (i) supports both one-time donations and recurring dues payments with flexible frequency, and (ii) enforces auditable, tamper-evident bookkeeping with automated reconciliation against external gateway events. The deployment context is the Universitas Indonesia campus and similar Indonesian nonprofit groups, where payment methods include local e-wallets and Midtrans as well as international cards via Stripe. Organizational needs include PDF receipt generation in Bahasa Indonesia, role-based invoice issuance, and traceable ledger entries for financial officers.

To address these needs, we present DonasiPlus-Laravel and summarize our contributions as follows:
- An implemented Laravel 8 application integrating Stripe and Midtrans via secure webhook verification with HMAC checking and replay protection.
- A transaction model with atomic ledger operations, FIFO reconciliation rules, and clear formulas for balance updates and cost-per-transaction accounting.
- A background processing architecture using Redis queues and Laravel Horizon with exponential backoff for retry semantics, meeting realistic latency targets ($T_{api}\approx120\,\mathrm{ms}$).
- A role-based access control (RBAC) model, immutable audit logs stored in append-only tables, and receipts generation supporting PDF and email delivery.
- A reproducible evaluation on a 4 vCPU, 8 GB VM with PostgreSQL primary-replica configuration and a six-month pilot at Universitas Indonesia showing 95.4% automated reconciliation accuracy and a 78% reduction in manual work hours.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the related literature on donation platforms, payment gateway integration, and web security practices. Section III details the system design, hardware and software configuration, data model, and control strategies including the reconciliation algorithm. Section IV presents the experimental setup, performance results, ablation studies, and a reliability assessment. Section V concludes with lessons learned, limitations, and future directions for multi-tenant and formal audit capabilities.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: We organize related work into three threads: donation platforms and nonprofit software, payment gateway integration and webhook reliability, and web application security and auditability. Representative works span industrial systems and academic studies; we highlight practical limitations relevant to our design choices.

content.text: Commercial donation platforms (e.g., Donorbox, GoFundMe) offer easy front-ends for one-time donations but rarely provide university-level membership management with recurring dues linked to member records [1][9]. Donorbox emphasizes simplicity, yet its reconciliation for offline donations or local Indonesian e-wallets is limited. Research prototypes such as microdonation frameworks propose efficient routing and bandit-based matching for donor campaigns but omit the accounting primitives required for monthly dues [10][11]. Academic systems that address nonprofit accounting focus on audit models and ledger immutability but are not designed for production web stacks like Laravel that need to integrate with local gateways and deliver receipts in Bahasa Indonesia [12].

content.text: Fig. 1 contrasts DonasiPlus-Laravel with common commercial offerings: the key technical distinctions are native support for Midtrans, an explicit reconciliation layer, and append-only audit storage. These are necessary in Indonesian deployments where offline receipts and multiple local payment channels are common. The figure motivates our focus on transactional correctness and local gateway compatibility, which other platforms address only partially.

Reliable integration with payment gateways requires secure webhook handling, idempotency, and replay protection [3][5][13]. Industry guidance from Stripe and Midtrans emphasizes the use of signatures and HMAC verification to ensure payload authenticity; however, academic studies show that webhook reliability hinges on queueing strategies and retry semantics for transient network faults [6][14]. Prior work on webhook-driven systems suggests exponential backoff and persistent queues to avoid lost events, but most open-source projects omit formal analysis of queue sizing under peak load [7]. Our system mixes Redis queues with Laravel Horizon-based workers to achieve controlled concurrency and visibility, drawing on these prior techniques but focusing on idempotent ledger writes that guarantee consistency even with duplicate webhooks.

Security and traceability in donation systems involve access control, data minimization, and tamper-evident logging. Techniques such as append-only audit tables, HMAC-signed receipts, and role separation for finance staff are standard in payment systems [15][16]. Academic approaches add cryptographic timestamping and Merkle trees for immutable logs; however, these add complexity and are rarely adopted by small organizations due to operational overhead [12][17]. We balance practicality and security by implementing RBAC through Laravel policies, storing immutable audit rows with event metadata (user, timestamp, signature), and supporting optional periodic export for external auditors. This combination adheres to engineering constraints in university deployments while providing a path toward stronger cryptographic attestations in future work.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section describes the overall architecture, hardware, data model, reconciliation algorithm, and the communication pipeline that binds payment gateways to ledger updates.

content.text: DonasiPlus-Laravel adopts a layered architecture: a Laravel 8 application hosts controllers and REST APIs, PostgreSQL 13 serves as the primary ledger store with synchronous replication to a read replica, Redis provides queueing and caching, and Nginx plus a load balancer front the application servers. The application supports both web and PWA mobile clients, and uses OAuth2-compatible authentication for SSO with Universitas Indonesia services. External integrations include Stripe for international card payments and Midtrans for local e-wallets and bank transfers. Webhooks from gateways are verified using HMAC-SHA256 signatures and processed by dedicated queue workers to ensure idempotent ledger updates [3][5].

content.text: The architecture enforces transaction boundaries at the application level: controller endpoints create a Transaction record in a pending state, call the payment provider API via an HTTP client, and await webhook confirmation. The webhook handler is idempotent: it matches provider event IDs to existing transactions and atomically transitions ledger entries to settled. Expected API call latency is $T_{api}=120$ ms on our test VM and webhook median latency is $T_{webhook}=80$ ms when gateways operate nominally. These latency targets guided our queue sizing and worker pool configuration in the evaluation section.

Equation (1) defines the ledger balance update: $B_t$ is the ledger balance at time $t$, $D_i$ enumerates donation inflows, and $W_j$ enumerates withdrawals or transfers. The implementation enforces this relationship using atomic database transactions so that concurrent webhook arrivals do not produce inconsistent $B_t$ values.

The reference deployment used in experiments replicates a typical small organizational hosting setup: a 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM virtual machine hosted on a Jakarta cloud provider, a PostgreSQL primary with a streamed replica, and a Redis server for queueing. For development and local gateway testing we also used Raspberry Pi 4 edge nodes for NFC card reader integration and an Arduino Uno prototype bridging older POS hardware. The system runs Ubuntu Server 20.04, PHP 8.0, Composer for dependency management, Nginx 1.18, and PostgreSQL 13 with pglogical for replication in the pilot setup at Universitas Indonesia's Computer Engineering lab.

section3c.title: Algorithm and Control Strategy (Reconciliation and Queues)

content.text: The core algorithmic component is the reconciliation engine that maps external payment provider events to internal ledger transactions. The engine uses FIFO matching for batched payouts, idempotent event handling, and a cost allocation procedure for gateway fees. A transaction lifecycle comprises: Created (pending), Authorized, Settled (on webhook confirmation), and Reconciled (match to banking payout). For recurring dues, the scheduler creates pending invoices and enqueues charge jobs. Background workers perform network calls and update statuses based on webhook receipts. The queue semantics rely on Redis lists and Laravel Horizon for visibility and concurrency control. Retry logic implements exponential backoff with capped attempts to avoid infinite retry storms.

Equation (2) defines exponential backoff where $t_0$ is the base interval and $k$ is the retry attempt index. We cap $k$ at 3 in production to limit duplicate charges and reconcile retries with human review when necessary. The implementation uses Horizon job attempts configuration and a custom middleware to compute $t_{retry}(k)$ before re-queuing.

Equation (3) defines success rate $\\eta$ used in our evaluation: $N_{\\mathrm{success}}$ counts transactions successfully reconciled without manual intervention, while $N_{\\mathrm{total}}$ counts total attempted transactions. In our pilot, $N_{\\mathrm{total}}$ was 2,500 transactions over six months and $\\eta$ computed to 95.4% for automated reconciliation.

Practical implementation details include idempotency keys: every initiated payment stores a provider idempotency key $k_{id}$ that is submitted to the gateway. The webhook handler checks $k_{id}$ and provider event ID to ensure a single ledger entry per real payment. For multi-currency donations we store amounts in smallest currency units and maintain a currency column alongside exchange rate metadata where applicable.

content.text: Communication across components uses HTTPS with TLS 1.2+, JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for APIs, and signed webhooks for provider events. The pipeline enforces verification: the webhook payload is checked against a stored secret using HMAC-SHA256 and the timestamp is validated to prevent replay. Once verified, the event is enqueued and processed by a worker that performs an atomic update within a database transaction. For reporting, we maintain denormalized reporting tables updated asynchronously to avoid read-write contention on the ledger.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate DonasiPlus-Laravel with controlled synthetic tests and a six-month pilot at Universitas Indonesia student organizations. Metrics include reconciliation accuracy, latency, throughput, and operational reduction in manual tasks.

content.text: The testbed comprises a 4 vCPU, 8 GB VM running Ubuntu 20.04 hosting the Laravel application behind Nginx, a PostgreSQL 13 primary with one replica, and a Redis 6 instance for job queues. External two gateways were exercised: Stripe (test mode) and Midtrans sandbox. Synthetic load tests used Locust 2.0 with up to 200 concurrent users generating donation and dues payment flows over 30-minute runs. For the pilot, DonasiPlus was deployed in March 2025 at Universitas Indonesia with 12 student organizations using the system for dues collection and occasional fundraising campaigns.

content.text: Main results include throughput, latency, reconciliation accuracy, and cost-per-transaction estimates. Under the synthetic load test with Locust, the system sustained 200 transactions per minute ($N_{tx}=12{,}000$ per hour scaled) with average end-to-end latency $T_{total}=T_{api}+T_{webhook}+T_{db}+T_{queue}\approx320$ ms in typical runs. The majority of delay was network-bound: $T_{api}=120$ ms and $T_{webhook}=80$ ms median. The reconciliation engine matched $N_{success}=2{,}385$ out of $N_{total}=2{,}500$ automated events in the pilot, giving $\\eta=95.4\%$ automated reconciliation. Manual resolution covered the remaining 114 transactions, typically due to gateway timeout or offline bank transfers requiring human verification.
content.Title: Performance Results

content.text: Table III consolidates the key performance numbers observed during controlled experiments and pilot operations. Reconciliation accuracy of 95.4% corresponds to a 78% reduction in manual reconciliation time compared to spreadsheet-based workflows measured in the pilot: average monthly reconciliation time dropped from 25 hours to 5.5 hours per organization. The primary reasons for manual interventions were offline bank transfers with delayed confirmation and occasional Midtrans sandbox webhook ordering issues.

content.text: Equation (5) gives cost per transaction $C_{\\mathrm{tx}}$ as the monthly infrastructure cost plus gateway fees divided by total transactions $N_{\\mathrm{tx}}$. For our pilot, using monthly infrastructure cost $C_{\\mathrm{infra}}=2{,}400{,}000$ IDR, gateway fees averaging 2.9% plus fixed 2,500 IDR per transaction, and $N_{\\mathrm{tx}}=12{,}000$ monthly transactions, we measure $C_{\\mathrm{tx}}$ around 200 IDR per transaction excluding variable sponsorship flows.

Beyond raw metrics, operational qualitative gains were significant: finance officers reported streamlined month-end reporting, automated PDF receipts reduced invoice disputes, and audit logs simplified spot checks. One point that matters in deployment is gateway SLA: during a Midtrans partial outage on 2025-02-14 the system recorded delayed webhooks which required manual fallback procedures. We discuss this reliability aspect next.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compare DonasiPlus-Laravel with two representative baselines: Method A (a monolithic PHP application without queueing) and Method B (commercial donation platform tailored to international donors). The ablation study disables Redis queueing and measures effect on latency and reconciliation. Without queues, average API latency rose to 420 ms under load and reconciliation accuracy fell to 87.6% due to missed or out-of-order webhook processing. Enabling Redis queues and Horizon reduced latency and improved idempotent handling.

content.text: We conducted a 90-day reliability study and stress test focused on webhook delivery and database stability. The system logged daily transactions and uptime; overall uptime measured at 99.92% with a notable payment gateway outage on 2025-02-14. Stress tests used stepwise concurrency increases to a 1,200 tpm peak sustained for five minutes; the platform degraded gracefully, with queue backlogs reaching a maximum depth of 1,800 jobs which were drained in under 12 minutes after peak subsided thanks to Horizon workers autoscaling. Persistent issues arose when gateway sandbox environments reordered events under peak load, prompting the addition of event sequence checks in reconciliation.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: This paper presented DonasiPlus-Laravel, a practical, implemented system for managing membership dues and donations tailored to Indonesian nonprofits and university organizations. We integrated Laravel 8 with Stripe and Midtrans, implemented HMAC-signed webhook verification, atomic ledger updates, Redis-based background processing, and append-only audit logs. Empirical evaluation on a 4 vCPU, 8 GB VM with PostgreSQL primary-replica demonstrated automated reconciliation accuracy of 95.4%, average API latency $T_{api}=120$ ms, sustained throughput of 200 transactions per minute, and an observed reduction in manual reconciliation time by 78% during a six-month pilot at Universitas Indonesia.

Despite these results, several limitations remain. First, gateway outages (e.g., Midtrans partial downtime on 2025-02-14) require robust fallback operational procedures; DonasiPlus currently surfaces such events and queues retries but does not perform financial guarantee arbitration. Second, the system does not yet provide full cryptographic attestation for external audits (e.g., Merkle proofs), which would be necessary for larger NGOs seeking formal certification. Third, multi-tenant isolation at scale requires further design to prevent noisy neighbor effects in shared Redis or database resources.

Planned future work includes (i) implementing optional cryptographic audit proofs and time-stamping for receipts, (ii) adding formal double-entry accounting modules interoperable with popular accounting software and AIS exports, and (iii) extending the platform to multi-tenant SaaS with per-tenant resource quotas and stricter isolation. We will also pursue collaboration with Universitas Indonesia's accounting department to validate compliance with statutory reporting requirements for non-profit organizations in Indonesia.

In sum, DonasiPlus-Laravel demonstrates that careful engineering of webhook verification, idempotent reconciliation, and queue-driven background processing can significantly reduce manual work and improve transparency in dues and donation management for small-to-medium organizations.
